sentence.rule: The usual order is subject + verb + object (SVO).
Verb endings often make the subject clear, especially eu and nós.
Use ser for identity and defining traits. Use estar for states and locations.
sentence.translation: I am a student. I am tired.

sentence.rule: Put não directly before the verb.
Word order usually stays the same. Intonation marks the question.
Put onde, quando, como, por que or quanto near the start.
In Brazilian Portuguese, você takes third-person forms and a gente means we with a singular verb.
Articles agree in gender and number: o, a, os, as, um, uma.
Adjectives usually agree with the noun in gender and number.
Most words take -s, but spelling and stress can change.
sentence.translation: Two buses and three bread rolls.

sentence.rule: Use de + person or pronoun to show possession.
Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner.
de combines with articles: do, da, dos, das.
em combines with articles: no, na, nos, nas.
a combines with o and os as ao and aos.
sentence.translation: I am going to the market.

sentence.rule: Pra is the common spoken form of para.
Everyday commands often use forms such as fala, olha, espera and vem.
Use pode + infinitive or por favor.
In everyday Brazilian speech, tem often means there is or there are.
Já often asks or states whether something has happened.
Use a present form of ir + infinitive for plans and predictions.
sentence.translation: I am going to call tomorrow.

sentence.rule: Use estar + gerund for an action in progress.
Use mais or menos + adjective + que.
sentence.example: Este é mais barato que aquele.
sentence.translation: This one is cheaper than that one.

sentence.rule: -inho and -inha can express small size, affection or intensity.
sentence.translation: It is very close to here.

sentence.rule: Use e, mas, porque, então and também to connect ideas.
sentence.translation: I am tired, but I am going.

sentence.rule: Use né? to seek agreement or confirmation in casual speech.
sentence.translation: It is hot today, isn't it?

tracks.title: Sounds that change meaning
tracks.description: Hear and produce the contrasts that most affect understanding.

tracks.title: Syllables, rhythm and stress
tracks.description: Break words and phrases into repeatable chunks.

tracks.title: Fast reading rules
tracks.description: Use frequent patterns without memorizing every exception.

tracks.title: Natural Brazilian speech
tracks.description: Recognize reductions and regional sounds without chasing perfection.

tracks.title: Sentence builder
tracks.description: Build useful messages from a few reliable parts.

tracks.title: Tenses on one line
tracks.description: Say now, before and after with the most useful forms.

lessons.title: Open and closed vowels
lessons.goal: Hear the difference in stressed E and O.
lessons.rule: Brazilian Portuguese keeps several vowel qualities. A clearer stressed vowel often matters more than perfect consonants.

lessons.title: Nasal vowels
lessons.goal: Let air pass through the nose without adding a hard N.
lessons.rule: The tilde and vowels before M or N often signal nasal sound.

lessons.title: R and RR
lessons.goal: Recognize strong and soft Brazilian R.
lessons.rule: Initial R and RR are usually strong. A single R between vowels is a quick tap.
lessons.sayMeaning: The car is on the street.

lessons.title: LH, NH, TI and DI
lessons.goal: Produce four high-value Brazilian combinations.
lessons.rule: LH and NH are single sound units. In much of Brazil, ti and di may be realized as /tʃi/ and /dʒi/.

lessons.title: Clean vowel blocks
lessons.goal: Find one main vowel in each syllable.
lessons.rule: Portuguese syllables are often clearer and more even than English syllables.
lessons.say: O mercado fica perto de casa.

lessons.title: Find the stressed block
lessons.goal: Make one syllable stronger.
lessons.rule: Accent marks show stress. Without a mark, common ending patterns predict it.

lessons.title: Keep useful final sounds
lessons.goal: Recognize final L, R and S.
lessons.rule: Final L often sounds close to W. Final R varies by region. Final S marks plurals and verb forms.

lessons.title: Stress the message words
lessons.goal: Make the important words easy to hear.
lessons.rule: Give extra force to the verb and key noun. Small words can stay light.

lessons.title: C and QU
lessons.goal: Choose the common C sound from the next vowel.
lessons.rule: C before E or I sounds like S. C before A, O or U sounds like K. QU often keeps the K sound before E or I.

lessons.title: G and GU
lessons.goal: Recognize hard and soft G.
lessons.rule: G before E or I is soft. GU keeps a hard G before E or I.

lessons.title: S, SS and Z
lessons.goal: Use position to predict the sound.
lessons.rule: A single S between vowels often sounds like Z. SS keeps the S sound.
lessons.sayMeaning: I will stop by your house.

lessons.title: X and CH
lessons.goal: Learn these patterns by familiar words.
lessons.rule: X has several sounds, so store it with the word. CH is usually one SH-like sound.
lessons.sayMeaning: The key is in the taxi.

lessons.title: Unstressed E and O
lessons.goal: Recognize vowels that become smaller at word endings.
lessons.rule: In many Brazilian accents, final E approaches I and final O approaches U.

lessons.title: Regional final R
lessons.goal: Understand more than one correct Brazilian R.
lessons.rule: Final R may sound strong, soft or nearly disappear. Focus on recognizing the word.
lessons.sayMeaning: I want to eat and leave.

lessons.title: Recognize everyday reductions
lessons.goal: Understand pra, tá, cê and a gente.
lessons.rule: You may answer with standard forms first. Learn reductions mainly so real speech stops sounding too fast.

lessons.title: Speak in chunks
lessons.goal: Pause where the meaning closes.
lessons.rule: Short chunks make imperfect speech much easier to understand.

examples.meaning: I want / to pay by card

lessons.title: Drop the subject when clear
lessons.goal: Use the verb as the center of the message.
lessons.rule: Portuguese verb forms often make eu clear. Quero and preciso already work as strong message starters.

lessons.title: Who, action, thing
lessons.goal: Build subject + verb + object.
lessons.rule: This basic order works for most first conversations.

lessons.title: Put não before the verb
lessons.goal: Make a clear negative with one word.
lessons.rule: Use não directly before the verb. No auxiliary is needed.

lessons.title: Question frames
lessons.goal: Ask for information with fixed frames.
lessons.rule: Intonation and a question word can turn the familiar sentence into a question.

lessons.title: Present for routine and now
lessons.goal: Use one form for many present situations.
lessons.rule: Use the simple present for routines. For an action in progress now, use estar plus the gerund.

examples.text: A gente espera / A gente está esperando
examples.meaning: We wait; for an action in progress: We are waiting

lessons.title: Emphasize action in progress
lessons.goal: Use estar + gerund only when useful.
lessons.rule: Use estou, está or estamos plus -ando, -endo or -indo to emphasize right now.

lessons.title: Finished past
lessons.goal: Tell what happened with a completed past form.
lessons.rule: Memorize a few high-value forms first: fui, fiz, tive, falei and liguei.
lessons.sayMeaning: I went to the doctor yesterday.

lessons.title: Future with ir
lessons.goal: Say the next step with ir + infinitive.
lessons.rule: Vou, vai and vamos plus the base verb cover most practical future plans.
lessons.sayMeaning: I am going to call tomorrow.
